Part I: From Nothingness to Numeration Manuscript

Many ancient civilizations, including India, had their own version of zero or a zero-like concept or symbol as a representative of ‘nothingness’; some as a philosophical conundrum, others even in a practical sense, such as a gap on their counting board. But except in India, none of these early and somewhat hesitant concepts ultimately matured to their true mathematical potential.

To be Contd.This first part of a two-part series traces that remarkable passage from philosophy to numeration. Part II will follow śūnya into written mathematics, culminating in the Bakhshali manuscript and its enigmatic bold dot, whose age remains debated.

Editor’s Note

Few ideas have transformed human thought as profoundly as zero. Yet zero did not enter mathematics fully formed. The concept of śūnya — emptiness, absence, the void — has its roots in ancient India, where it was explored philosophically long before it became a mathematical object.

Its development was gradual. India already possessed a sophisticated decimal system, but spoken numbers could simply omit an empty place and therefore required no symbol for zero. Once numbers began to be written positionally, however, an empty place had to be marked. Zero first served that practical role as a placeholder; only later did it come to be treated as a number in its own right.

Is zero only the nothingness forever so present with us?
It’s boundless too that our Rishis felt — the ananta, the infinitas —
A singularity containing the entire creation before the elemental spark —
The brightest light of our consciousness and the darkest of the dark
It has no beginning, this śūnya — and in essence it doesn’t have an end
Open only to our perception, its disposition is cryptically explained
In the Nāsadiya Sukta of the Rgveda — serving as a lighthouse on the shore
Of the ocean of wisdom to all naive navigators now after or before.1

1 Taken from the book Much Ado About Nothing by the present author, published on 6th March 2021 by Vivekananda Center for Research (ISBN: 978-81-950156-5-8), with due acknowledgment to Mr. Bijayaditya Chakraborty, who transliterated the original Bengali poem by Mrs. Madhumita Mukhopadhyay.

Introduction

Many ancient civilizations, including India, had their own version of zero or a zero-like concept or symbol as a representative of ‘nothingness’; some as a philosophical conundrum, others even in a practical sense, such as a gap on their counting board. But except in India, none of these early and somewhat hesitant concepts ultimately matured to their true mathematical potential.

Today, it is generally accepted worldwide that this peerless concept of a decimal place-value system of enumeration, in tandem with the true zero of our present-day mathematics, evolved in ancient India.

Initially philosophically nurtured and analyzed during the early periods of oral tradition in India by several different schools of thought, eventually, at some point in time, the concept reflected in the Sanskrit word śūnya was transformed into a numeral for mathematical expression of ‘nothing’. Perhaps later, it bloomed into its full potential as a number, kha, an integer on which mathematical operations can be performed.

Indeed, this unique feature makes kha, the Indian zero, the true progenitor of our modern ‘mathematical zero’.

However, kha literally means sky, which Sanskrit also calls śūnya. One suggested derivation of this word is from śūnā [+ yat], which is the past participle of the root śvī, which means ‘to swell’ or ‘to expand’, and there from by semantic extension ‘hollow’. In the Ṛgveda, one may find another meaning — ‘the sense of lack or deficiency’. The two different meanings were fused to give śūnya a single sense of absence or emptiness with the potential for growth, a womb-like hollow, ready to receive and swell.

(It is interesting to note that the root of the word Brahmā is brinh, which also means ‘to swell’ or ‘to expand’.)

The exact time frame for this gradual evolution from concept to number is still hotly debated. A recent controversy in this direction concerns contradictory radiocarbon dating results for the famous Bakhshali manuscript: the Bodleian Library of Oxford dated it first in 2017 and again, under secrecy, in 2024.

The Bakhshali manuscript is the first known mathematical writing of Indian origin to contain a symbol for ‘written’ zero (in the form of a bold dot) in numerous arithmetical calculations, where numbers are written in the decimal place-value system. It was discovered near a well in 1881 by chance when a farmer in the village of Bakhshali (Figure 1) in British India was trying to level a piece of land to prepare it for cultivation.

The site was about 50 miles from Peshawar and 150 miles from Kabul in present-day Pakistan, known to be a part of the erstwhile Gāndhāra region and was within 70 miles of Takśasilā, the famous ancient seat of learning that thrived from 1000 BCE before being plundered multiple times and finally destroyed completely by the Huna invaders in around the 5th Cent. CE.

Written in ink on birch bark, it is an incomplete document, neither having the beginning nor the end of the actual work, consisting of about 70 partially mutilated fragments. A greater part was reported to be destroyed while it was dug up by the farmer, from where it lay buried between huge stones.

The illiterate farmer luckily did not throw away the bunch, considering it useless; rather, he handed it over to the landlord Mia Anwanuddin, a local inspector of police, who, unable to understand the meanings of the scribbling on it, deposited it with the then British resident commissioner of Mardan.

After a few more welcome changes of hands, it ultimately reached Gen. Alexander Cunningham, the founder of the Archaeological Survey of India, who arranged to send the manuscript to Dr. R. Hoernle, director of Calcutta Madrasa, for examination and publication. Orientalist Dr. Hoernle gave a short description of it before the Asiatic Society of Bengal in 1883, then worked on it extensively and presented its contents at international conferences in Germany.

Finally, in 1902, after finishing his research, he presented it to the Bodleian Library of Oxford, where this priceless document is presently kept. The Bodleian mounted the manuscript leaves between sheets of mica and placed them in an album (Figure 2). It is now in extremely fragile condition, having disintegrated into thousands of small fragments within the casing.

Fortunately, advanced reprographic technology has allowed researchers to reproduce exact digital images of both sides of the manuscript pages, making them available for expert examination.

In mid-2017, a team of experts from the Bodleian Library and the Oxford Radiocarbon Accelerator Unit collaborated on radiocarbon dating (14C analysis) of the manuscript. Five samples were extracted from the birch bark manuscript, avoiding the inked portion; three were analyzed, following the state-of-the-art technological protocol required for such an experiment.

The result, as declared by Oxford Mathematics Professor Marcus du Sautoy on YouTube, revealed (though never formally published for peer review) that the three samples tested, surprisingly dated from different centuries, at least 500 years apart: Folio 16 from 224 to 383 CE, Folio 17 from 680 to 779 CE, and Folio 33 from 885 to 993 CE [1].

Explaining this unexpected time gap, which does not conform to the earlier proposed dating by some influential experts in this field, who want to place the origin of written Indian zero at a later date, has given rise to a flurry of activities, as this document is clearly associated with the history of a ‘written zero symbol’ in India.

Origin of Numbers

The concept of numbers gradually evolved in early human civilizations as an abstraction of the physical process of counting tangible objects. At this stage, one does not need the ‘number zero’ because counting begins at one. Only at a more mature stage of mental development, the idea of the number zero is introduced, usually depicted through a process of step-by-step subtraction, as a number representing ‘nothingness’.

While we now take only a few years to assimilate these ideas during our formative years, this journey from concrete to abstract initially took mankind thousands of years. However, the exact time frame, as well as the geographical location of its philosophical origin as an abstract representation of conceptual nothingness, and subsequent gradual evolution to a fully bloomed number, an integer, are still debated.

But it is generally accepted worldwide, among a majority of scholars and common folk alike, that the decimal (i.e., base 10) place value system of enumeration in tandem with the concept of number ‘zero’ (its present universal symbol, 0, is a later Indian development) was first thought of at some point of time in ancient India, perhaps philosophically to begin with and then mathematically, most possibly at different time epochs. It is indeed a peerless gift of Indian civilization to the world.

Tracing the Footsteps of Indian Zero

The word ‘zero’ originated from the Sanskrit word śūnya, which was only one of the several synonyms such as kha, ākāsha, gagana, ananta, pūrna and many others (called bhūtasamkhyā) used to represent the concept; a dichotomy as well as a simultaneity between nothing and everything, the zero of void and that of all-pervading fathomless infinite, hinted through the simile of the vast and limitless expanse of the sky.

Initially, in the pre-Common Era days of oral tradition in India, one finds several examples of decimal place value-based Sanskrit number names in early Vedic Indian scriptures from the Rgveda onward. However, these examples were without any exclusive reference to any ‘number zero’, since such a thing is not required in uttering the names of numbers larger than zero, until, of course, someone wanted to specifically refer to the ‘number zero’ itself.

The earliest known case appears in Piṅgala’s chandasūtra, composed sometime in the third century BCE, where a zero occurring as a label in a prosodic discussion steeped in mathematical spirit is referred to by the name śūnya (see Figure 3).

Zero as a numerical symbol becomes indispensable only when one starts writing numbers in a place-value-based system. The absence of any other digit in one or more ‘places’ of a written number cannot otherwise be tackled successfully.

Of course, one may think of the naive way of leaving a gap at the requisite place or places, but that will surely confuse later readers, particularly if such a requirement occurs at successive median places or even at the end of the number, as the history of similar attempts in different civilizations (e.g., Babylonian and Chinese) over several centuries clearly testify [2].

One of the important mathematical roles of zero is that of a placeholder, where it allows the other digits (say from 1 to 9 as in the decimal place value system), to take their own ‘places’ in the written representation of a number, so as to be able to distinguish between, say, 15, 105, and 100,005.

With the passage of time, this zero was eventually appreciated as an independent numeral, a number in its own right, on the same footing with any of the other digits, a number for the mathematical expression of ‘nothing’, with which or on which one can operate mathematically, as we use it today, for example, 1 − 1 = 0, or 1 + 0 = 1. And this later phase of its evolution is purely Indian in origin.

Philosophical Backbone of Indian Zero

In ancient Vedic India, only the oral tradition (śruti) of knowledge transmission prevailed. This society was amazingly rich in lofty philosophical ideas and thoughts, as testified by the Vedas, Upaniṣads, and many other texts of the Vedic corpus, as well as by later Buddhist and Jaina texts.

However, unlike Greece (who were kind of horrified by the idea of the void and hence with the number zero [2]), philosophers of every school of thought in India seemed to have toyed freely with the concept of nothingness and embraced the idea of complete void.

For example, in the Tantra, one finds the eternal divine creator Niṣkala (partless) Shiva, the undifferentiated formless omnipotence, the Lord Shiva, who creates this whole universe from the void and destroys his creation into the void again and again.

From the Nāsadiya sūkta of the Rgveda (Figure 4), where the Vedic seer is philosophically trying to imagine the nature of the complete vacuum before the creation of the universe [2], to the concept of māyā (illusory non-existence in reality) in Vedānta philosophy, from the concept of abhāva (absence) of the Nyāya school, to the Śūnyavāda (doctrine of devoidness) of Nāgārjuna of the Madhyamaka school of Mahāyāna Buddhism.

In this Buddhist framework, the highest form of knowledge, i.e., prajñāpāramitā, is attributed to the perception of everything phenomenal or worldly as śūnya; the spiritual attainment of this sense of śūnyatā, the pure void (the state of catuṣkoṭi vinirmukta) being nirvāna (the ultimate emancipation) as seen from the teachings of Mulamadhyamakakārikā.

It appears very likely that the thread of the rich philosophical and socio-academic ambiances of Indian Antiquity was quite pregnant with the immensity of the concept of śūnya, – a dichotomy as well as a simultaneity between ‘nothing’ and ‘everything’.

Hindu culture worshiped the supreme God Brahma as eṣa śuddha śūnya śāntah (oh thy pure, calm, void incarnate) in one of the Upaniṣads and in another as anoroṇian mahatomahiān, (minuter than the minutest, and yet simultaneously larger than the largest); the śūnya (zero) of void and that of an all-pervading fathomless pūrna (infinite wholeness) seemed to be merely two sides of the same coin in their philosophical outlook.

In this society, where mathematics, an aparāvidyā (worldly knowledge) that was treated with utmost importance, to be considered at the helm of all the Vedānga śāstras (like the crest of a peacock or the gem on the hood of a serpent), when mathematicians felt or declared the necessity of having a numeral for śūnya, society at large never contradicted the idea or tried to resist it, contrary to what was the case in Greece, where Aristotelian dictum went against any possible vacuum in nature and hence against zero as a number.

Antiquity of Indian Decimal Place Value System

To appreciate the real importance of the role of zero, it has to be considered in tandem with the decimal (daśa) place value system prevailing in India during the Vedic age (c. 1200 BCE) or even earlier. Yāskācharya, in his Nirukta (etymology, one of the six limbs of the Vedas) (c. 600 BCE), traced the root of daśa (10) to the verb dṛś (to see), and pointed out that the use of 10 is seen in the formation of subsequent numbers.

It clearly shows that the status of the number 10 was not like the other ankas (digits), from eka (1), dvi (2), through nava (9).

One early passive reference to the decimal place value system is seen in a different context in the first-century CE Buddhist Madhyamaka school text Abhidharmakoṣa by Basumitra. While illustrating the theory of dharmas (elements or factors), he used the comparison “like a marker (vartikā) in reckoning, which in the unit position has the value of a unit, in the hundreds position that of a hundred and in thousands position that of a thousand” [3].

A strikingly similar statement, but from a completely different perspective, is also found later in the seventh century CE: the Vyāsabhāṣya of the Yogasūtra by Patanjali.

However, if one wants to find this place value principle in an exclusively mathematical text, the earliest one known is Āryabhaṭiya [499 CE] by Āryabhaṭa of Kusumpura (near present-day Patna of Bihar, India). He clearly enunciated the decimal place names from unit (eka), 10 (daśa) up to the ninth power of 10 (brinda), stating clearly that at every stage the next higher place is 10 times (daśagunam) the previous one.

These earlier examples, however, show that the decimal system was conceptualized and in vogue long before in ancient India.

Indeed, it had gone well beyond the ninth power, with new single-word names coined for higher powers of ten. Various ancient texts reveal a penchant for naming larger and larger numbers in powers of 10, as if to assert a superior claim to numeracy before their audience. In the Śukla Yajurveda we find a mention of the 12th power of 10 (parārdha); in a Buddhist work, Lalitabistāra, the 53rd power of 10 (tallakṣhna); while in a Jaina text, Amalasiddhi, the 96th power of 10 (daśa-ananta) is mentioned.

Incidentally, it is well established today, thanks to the pioneering work of R. C. Gupta [4], that Āryabhaṭa’s algorithms for extraction of the square and cube roots of a number, that he preferred to present through a language-based scheme (in Ganitapada verses 4 and 5), can work only in a fully functional place value system with zero.

Most likely this fact, transmitted wrongly, has given rise to the common misinformation among generally educated Indian folk that Āryabhaṭa “invented” zero, since to date we do not have any information about an exclusive and systematic Indian text per se on mathematics, written before Āryabhaṭiya.

Amazingly, one may find about 3,000 decimal nomenclatures of number names in the Ṛgveda [circa 1500 BCE], which is astonishingly rich in words and phrases relating to numbers [Bavare 2013]. Starting from the nine primary numbers, i.e., the digits (aṇka) such as one (eka), two (dvi) up to nine (nava), it has the first nine multiples of ten: ten (daśa), twenty (viṃśati) up to 90 (navati), and also the powers of ten up to ayuta (the 4th power of ten).

The largest example is navatiṃnava sahasra (ninety [and] nine thousand). Many of these number names exhibit the “fundamental characteristics obligatory to an orally expressed decimal system,” as has been investigated at length by Bavare and Divakaran [5].

As Divakaran [6] points out, “the earliest Vedic texts show in an absolutely unambiguous manner that one can implement the place value paradigm just as effectively with spoken number names — as with number symbols. The rules for forming numbers above nine — serving the same purpose as the now-universal sequence in the written symbolic notation — had to be realized by applying rules of nominal composition: in other words, rules of grammar.”

However, there is no exclusive reference to the number zero to be found at this stage, as this was never required for oral treatment of number names, not even for the numbers like sata (hundred), sahasra (thousand) or, for example, a more complicated ṣaṣṭiṃ sahasrā navatiṃnava (sixty thousand ninety [and] nine), etc. This requirement became unavoidable only at a much later stage, when writing these numbers in a place value paradigm was necessary.

Number Names to Written Numerals

A. K. Dutta [7] observes: “To arrive at a written decimal notation from the above terminologies, one has to simply suppress the place names from a given numerical expression, provided one has an additional tenth numeral as a placeholder to indicate the possible absence of the nine numerals at certain places.

Thus one can conclude that the structure of the Sanskrit numeral system contains the key to the decimal place value system.” This in effect indicates the polynomial structural form of Sanskrit (decimal) number names, where suppressing the place names is equivalent to considering the ordered tuple made with the coefficients of the polynomial, as is done in polynomial ring theory in Modern Algebra.

In the first representation, some power(s) of the variable may remain absent (just as in an oral number name of a particular number, some place(s) may not feature at all), while in the second representation, the corresponding position(s) in the ordered tuple must be filled with zero(s) to indicate that polynomial correctly (respectively, when we have to write that particular number, the vacant places demand the placeholder zero).

Before the time of the Aśokan edicts [around the middle of the third century BCE], or the Nānāghaṭ inscription [second century BCE], no systematic written records are known to exist in India, although the Pāṇinian text Aṣṭādhyāyī (c. 5th century BCE) does cite the Sanskrit words lipikar/lipikari (meaning ‘scribe’ in both genders).

Here we set aside the case of Harappan seals, which is yet to be completely deciphered; indeed, even their status as a written language is being strongly challenged by Mukhopadhyay [8]. Thus, it is clear that a written symbol for zero (as a placeholder) evolved out of a place value system (decimal, in this case) at the point when written representation of the already perfected oral system became necessary.

And it is precisely here that we stumble upon a critical fact. The initial Indian written records available are almost all in the Prākrit language and Brāhmi script, written from left to right, be it a sermon on stone inscription (for example, the Sāsārām rock edict of Aśoka from circa 250 BCE) or an inscribed date on numerous metal coins. However, some stray Kharosthi examples were found, mostly in the erstwhile Gāndhāra region, now in Pakistan.

Written from right to left, the Kharosthi system of writing numerals was even more primitive compared to Brāhmi. Of course, there was no zero in it, and this script had no impact on the later development of written languages in India.

However, Brāhmi numerals (Figure 5), though basically grouped by ten and its powers (and hence decimal in spirit), were not written according to a positional (place value based) system. The system was multiplicative-additive in principle, and there was no numeral symbol for zero, as an additive system does not need it. Some 30 instances from the time of the Sātavāhana kingdom (c. 2nd century BCE) of south India were found in the Nānāghaṭ inscription (written in Sanskrit using Brāhmi script), in the Western Ghat region of India. For example, the number 24,400 is written as three symbols side by side from left to right, the symbols being those for 20,000, 4,000, and 400.

The question is, why did a civilization that had already perfected and excelled in the oral decimal (positional) place value system have an inferior additive presentation of the written numbers? Divakaran [9] recently proposed a plausible explanation to this long-standing mystery.

According to him, the Brāhmi numbers “are a faithful symbolic version of the rules for forming decimal number names that had held sway from the time of the Rgveda, i.e., of the polynomial representation, and they result from the slavish transcription of names to symbols.

They are not positional because they have not reduced a number to a list of its (polynomial) coefficients.” This approach indeed explains the missing Brāhmi zero, as it indicates that up to this period the written place value based notations were yet to be invented.

Numerals in Brāhmi script, while pointing to the continuing hold of the oral tradition on the then relatively recent shift to a written paradigm, played a bridging role between the existing Sanskrit oral nominal composition scheme of decimal nomenclatures and the later place value based written symbolic representation of those decimal numbers.

In summary, this article lays the foundations of the Bold Dot Zero saga. Indian thought had long been comfortable with śūnya as absence, emptiness, and potentiality; its spoken number system had developed a sophisticated decimal structure; and the transition from number names to written numerals had created the need for a sign to preserve an empty place. Yet conceptual readiness is not the same as historical evidence.

When did śūnya first enter mathematical language, and when did it acquire a visible form?

Part II will follow that trail through early Indian texts, Pāṇini’s suggestive grammatical ancestor of placeholder zero and Piṅgala’s mathematical use of śūnya. It will then turn to the Bakhshali manuscript, where the bold dot appears repeatedly within a working decimal place-value system, and examine the unresolved controversy over the manuscript’s date.

Parthasarathi Mukhopadhyay

Dr. Parthasarathi Mukhopadhyay is Associate Professor of Mathematics at Ramakrishna Mission Residential College (Autonomous), Narendrapur, West Bengal. A gold-medalist M.Sc. in Pure Mathematics, he earned his M.Phil. and Ph.D. from the University of Calcutta. His work spans mathematics and its history, with particular emphasis on zero, Pingala’s prosody, abstract algebra, and linear algebra; he has also translated Robert Kanigel’s The Man Who Knew Infinity into Bengali. He has published research papers, authored several books in English and Bengali, and delivered more than 200 invited lectures in India and abroad. In 2021, he established the permanent “ZERO GALLERY: The Nothing That Is” at his college and served as narrator for the documentary Genesis of Zero. His recent scholarship includes the chapter “From Shunya to Zero – An Enigmatic Odyssey” in the 2024 Brill volume The Origin and Significance of Zero: An Interdisciplinary Perspective.
